passages.where: The disciples see a man blind from birth and ask Jesus whose sin caused it, his or his parents'. Jesus rejects both answers: neither this man nor his parents sinned. The site's note says it plainly, because the verse has been used to hurt people: illness and disability are not punishment for sin, the person's own or anyone else's.

The psalm blesses the one who cares for the poor and promises that the LORD will sustain him on his sickbed. The speaker is ill himself, surrounded by people waiting for him to die. He prays for mercy and healing, and he trusts that God is present in the bed of sickness, not only after it.

James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them and anoint them with oil in the name of the Lord. Oil was a medicine in James's world, and the site's note observes that none of the ways Christians read this sets prayer against medical care. The sick person is told to ask for help, and the church is told to come.

A man with a skin disease, cut off from others by the law and by fear, kneels and says to Jesus, if you are willing, you can make me clean. Jesus is moved, reaches out and touches him, and says I am willing. Before the healing comes the touch that no one else would give.

Epaphroditus, sent by the Philippians to care for Paul, falls so ill that he nearly dies. Paul says God had mercy on him, and on Paul too, sparing him sorrow upon sorrow. He claims no miracle and no guarantee; he simply calls the recovery mercy, and admits how much the illness of a friend weighed on him.

In the closing greetings of his last letter, Paul mentions that he left his coworker Trophimus sick in Miletus. The apostle through whom God had healed others left his own friend sick, and he says so without embarrassment. Faithful people in Scripture were sometimes left ill.

In Jesus' picture of the final judgment, the King says that whoever visited the sick visited him. The verb is one the Greek Old Testament uses for God coming to care for his people. To sit with the sick is not a small kindness; Christ counts it as done to himself.

Paul admits plainly that the outer self is wasting away. In the same sentence he says the inner self is being renewed day by day. Scripture does not ask a sick person to pretend the body is not failing; it says that something else is happening at the same time.

Asaph had nearly lost his faith envying the healthy, carefree wicked. At the end of the psalm he says that his flesh and his heart may fail, but God is the strength of his heart and his portion forever. Many readers hear in it a hope that reaches past death itself.

In the middle of instructions about church leaders, Paul gives Timothy a piece of practical medical advice: stop drinking only water and use a little wine, because of your stomach and your frequent illnesses. The same apostle who prayed for the sick told a sick friend to use the medicine of his day.

misread.taken: “By His stripes we are healed” is sometimes taught as a guarantee that every believer may claim physical healing now, so that a sick Christian who is not healed must be lacking faith or missing a promise.
misread.says: Isaiah's song speaks of a Servant who was pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, whose punishment brought peace. The New Testament uses it two ways. Matthew sees verse 4 fulfilled in Jesus' healing of the sick (Matthew 8:17), and Peter quotes verse 5 about sin borne on the cross, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness (1 Peter 2:24). Christians differ on how much bodily healing God gives in this life, and all hope for the day of resurrection when every disease will be healed. No faithful reading turns the verse into a promise that faith guarantees recovery now, or into a charge against the sick who are not healed.

whole: If your illness, or the fear and guilt around it, has become too heavy to bear alone, tell someone you trust, and if you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Serious illness changes everything at once. There are appointments, tests and waiting rooms, treatments that can be as hard as the disease, money worries, work interrupted, and a body that no longer does what it did. Many people describe a loneliness that sets in when others do not know what to say, and a fear that is hard to name: of pain, of dependence, of what comes next. Christians often carry a further question underneath: is God punishing me, or have I not had enough faith?

Scripture answers that question clearly. When the disciples asked whose sin had caused a man's blindness, Jesus said neither. The book of Job exists in part to refuse the idea that suffering is always deserved. Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus, told Timothy to take something for his stomach, and prayed three times about his own affliction without being relieved of it, and no one in Scripture blames any of them. The Bible also refuses to make sickness small. It names the failing body honestly, records the cries of sick people in the Psalms, and calls death an enemy. Illness is part of a world that is not yet as God made it to be, and it is not a verdict on the one who suffers.

So wisdom looks like two things held together. Pray boldly for healing, as James tells the sick to do, and call the church to pray with you. And receive good medical care, which is one of the ordinary ways God heals; seeing a doctor is not a lack of faith. Let people come close: Jesus touched the man everyone else kept at a distance, and he counts every visit to the sick as a visit to himself. Tell the truth about how you are, to God and to a few trusted people. Bring your fear to God in the words the psalms give you, and do not wait to feel brave before you do.

The deepest hope Scripture offers the sick is not a guarantee of recovery but the presence of God in the sickbed and a future beyond it. Paul could say that even while the outer self wastes away, the inner self is being renewed day by day. Asaph, with flesh and heart failing, called God his portion forever. Many are healed, and Christians rightly give thanks. Many are not, and they are no less loved or less faithful. For all who belong to Christ, the last word is not the diagnosis but the resurrection, when the body itself will be raised and made whole.

differ.share: All Christians pray for the sick, believe that God can heal, welcome medicine as a good gift, and look to the resurrection when every disease will be healed. None of them teaches that a believer who is not healed lacked faith.

views.name: The anointing of the sick as a sacrament
views.body: The Catholic and Orthodox churches see in James 5 the basis of a sacrament, the anointing of the sick, in which the church prays over the seriously ill and anoints them.

views.name: Prayer and anointing by the elders
views.body: Many Protestants read the oil in James 5 as a medicine of James's day, a sign, or both, and do not count it a sacrament. Some of their churches still have the elders anoint the sick with oil and pray, as James describes; others pray for the sick without oil.

views.name: Gifts of healing today
views.body: Pentecostal, charismatic and other continuationist Christians hold that the gift of healing Paul names in 1 Corinthians 12 continues until Christ returns, and they pray expecting it. Cessationist Christians hold that such sign gifts served the founding of the church, while God still heals in answer to prayer and through ordinary means.

differ.after: All of them pray, all of them receive good medical care with thanks, and all of them leave the outcome in God's hands.

sit: Who could you let a little closer in this illness, and what would you want them to know?

prayer.lead: A short, honest prayer from a body in pain: be merciful, heal me, how long? Pray it as it stands; you do not need better words.

careLines.text: If you are ill, this psalm does not mean God is punishing you.
Please do not let anyone tell you that it does.
If your pain or guilt has become too heavy to bear alone, tell someone you trust.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
